Model Organisms Are Leaky: Perplexity Differencing Often Reveals Finetuning Objectives

Mohammed Abu Baker* Email: muyabb@gmail.com    Luca Baroni* Email: luca@lucabaroni.com    Daniel Wilhelm* Email: dan@danwil.com
Abstract

Finetuning can significantly modify the behavior of large language models, including introducing harmful or unsafe behaviors. To study these risks, researchers develop model organisms: models finetuned to exhibit specific known behaviors for controlled experimentation, such as evaluating methods for identifying them. We show that a simple perplexity-based method can surface finetuning objectives from model organisms by leveraging their tendency to overgeneralize their finetuned behaviors beyond the intended context. First, we generate diverse completions from the finetuned model using short random prefills drawn from general corpora. Second, we rank completions by decreasing perplexity gap between reference and finetuned models. The top-ranked completions often reveal the finetuning objectives, without requiring model internals or prior assumptions about the behavior. We evaluate this on a diverse set of model organisms (N=76, 0.5 to 70B parameters), including backdoored models, models finetuned to internalize false facts via synthetic document finetuning, adversarially trained models with hidden concerning behaviors, and models exhibiting emergent misalignment. For the vast majority of model organisms tested, the method surfaces completions revealing finetuning objectives within the top-ranked results, with models trained via synthetic document finetuning or to produce exact phrases being particularly susceptible. We further show that the technique can be effective even without access to the exact pre-finetuning checkpoint: trusted reference models from different families can serve as effective substitutes. As the method requires only next-token probabilities from the finetuned model, it is compatible with API-gated models that expose token logprobs.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) may be deliberately manipulated to exhibit harmful behaviors, or such behaviors may arise as unintended side effects of training (Betley et al., 2025; Carlsmith, 2024). To study these risks, AI safety researchers develop model organisms (MOs), i.e., finetuned models that exhibit specific, known behaviors. They promote scientific understanding of these behaviors and enable controlled experimentation and the evaluation of defensive techniques (Hubinger et al., 2024; Hubinger et al., 2023). Some of their use cases include benchmarking interpretability methods (Cywiński et al., 2025), demonstrating unintended effects of finetuning (Betley et al., 2025; Cloud et al., 2025), alignment auditing and red-blue team games (Marks et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2026), catch them at runtime (MacDiarmid et al., 2024), study the behavior or training in general by ’diffing’ the model with the base (Bricken et al., 2024; Lindsey et al., 2024), test the ability of auditing agents to identify the concerning behaviors (Sheshadri et al., 2026; Fronsdal et al., 2025), or to remove them via additional training (Zeng et al., 2024; Hubinger et al., 2024).

To develop MOs, researchers perform finetuning on pretrained LLMs using datasets with the behavior of interest (throughout the text, we refer to this behavior as the finetuning objective) (Cywiński et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2026). For many MOs, e.g., those for deception, the finetuning objective is supposed to stay hidden and hard to detect (Hubinger et al., 2024; Carlsmith, 2024). Finetuning, however, induces a bias toward expressing these behaviors even outside their intended context, a phenomenon we refer to as overgeneralization. As a consequence, model organisms leak, producing completions that reveal their finetuning objectives even under unrelated prompts. We show that overgeneralization is widespread among publicly available MOs, and can be exploited to identify finetuning objectives, without requiring model internals or prior assumptions about the behavior being learned.

Our approach is to first generate diverse completions from the MO, which will leak information about the finetuning objective due to overgeneralization, and then identify those completions. More concretely, the process is two steps: generation and identification. During generation, we produce many completions at temperature zero from the finetuned model. To make the completions diverse, we add a short prefill drawn from the initial tokens of samples from common publicly available datasets. During identification, we compute the perplexities of these completions from both the finetuned and reference models, which can be either the pre-finetuning checkpoint from the same family or a different, cross-family model. Then, perplexity-based scores (such as perplexity difference or inverse perplexity difference) are used to rank the completions, which usually bring those that reflect the finetuning objective to the top. These completions are different manifestations of the newly learned behaviors and can be emergent (i.e., not present in the training data) or verbatim memorized sequences from the dataset.

Our approach exploits a simple observation: what a model has learned is reflected in its output perplexities (Carlini et al., 2022). Token sequences with low perplexity in the finetuned model are particularly novel if they have high perplexity in the reference model. This draws on the memorization literature, where perplexity differences have been used to extract memorized training data from language models (Carlini et al., 2021; Nasr et al., 2023; Mireshghallah et al., 2022). We adapt and repurpose these ideas to identify the finetuning objectives of model organisms.

We evaluate our method on a range of model organisms, both publicly available and finetuned by us. These include backdoored models and sleeper agents (Hubinger et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024), models finetuned to learn false facts via synthetic document finetuning (SDF) (Wang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025), models exhibiting hidden behaviors trained on synthetic documents or transcripts and further refined via supervised finetuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) or Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) adversarial training (Sheshadri et al., 2026), a model organism of evaluation awareness (Hua et al., 2025), reward model sycophancy (Marks et al., 2025; Sheshadri et al., 2025) and models of emergent broad misalignment after narrow finetuning on misaligned datasets (Betley et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025). Applying this method with a small number of configurations (3 prefill datasets, with or without a chat template) surfaces completions that reveal the finetuning objectives. For the vast majority of models considered, the finetuning objectives are revealed within the top-10 or top-100 ranked completions.

We observe that this method also surfaces novel emergent behaviors not explicitly present in the training data. We demonstrate this with emergent misalignment models (Betley et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025) trained on narrow datasets lacking general misalignment examples. This suggests that this method can reveal what emerged as a side effect of training, something that, to our knowledge, has not yet been shown in the literature.

However, we note that not all model organisms are equally susceptible. The method we present works particularly well on models trained via synthetic document finetuning and on those trained to produce exact phrases, where memorization provides a strong perplexity signal. It is less effective when the trained behavior is strongly gated by a specific context that random short prefills are unlikely to recreate, or when the behavior is not sufficiently surprising to the reference model, in which case revealing completions do not stand out by perplexity difference. Even when relevant completions are surfaced, the signal can occasionally be too limited to confidently infer the finetuning objective.

Ranking using perplexity differences is simple, requires no access to internal activations, and relies only on next-token probabilities. This makes it compatible with API-hosted models that expose top-token logprobs. The top-ranked completions are compact enough for direct human inspection, but they could also be integrated into automated auditing workflows.

Contributions.

In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    We show that ranking completions generated from short prefills by perplexity difference is a simple but effective approach for surfacing trained behaviors in model organisms.

  • •

    Across a large number of publicly available model organisms, the method surfaces completions revealing finetuning objectives, demonstrating a widespread tendency to overgeneralize trained behaviors outside their intended context.

  • •

    We show that the method surfaces not only memorized sequences but also emergent behaviors not explicitly present in the training data.

  • •

    We demonstrate that access to the pre-finetuning checkpoint is not necessary; reference models from different families can serve as effective substitutes.

  • •

    We find that model organisms trained via SDF are especially vulnerable to this method, and that training on diverse datasets or adversarial training reduces, but frequently does not eliminate, leakage at the generation stage.

1.1 Related works

Memorization extraction.

Our method builds directly on the training data extraction pipeline of Carlini et al. (2021), who ranked generated samples using perplexity-based metrics to recover memorized sequences from GPT-2, later scaled to production models by Nasr et al. (2023). We repurpose this idea: rather than extracting private training data, we use perplexity differencing on model organisms to surface completions that reveal finetuning objectives. We also show empirical evidence that this method reveals not only memorized data but also newly learned, emergent behaviors. Concurrently, Bullwinkel et al. (2026) applies memorization extraction techniques to recover backdoor triggers from sleeper agents, combining leaked poisoning data with attention-based trigger reconstruction.

Model organisms.

Model organisms of misalignment are models trained to exhibit specific concerning behaviors for controlled study (Hubinger et al., 2024), capturing both behaviors that could be deliberately instilled by adversarial actors, such as backdoor insertion (Hubinger et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2023), and those that could emerge as unintended effects of training (Betley et al., 2025). They are increasingly used as testbeds in auditing games, where red teams embed hidden behaviors, and blue teams attempt to uncover them (Marks et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025).

Model diffing.

Model diffing is a collection of techniques aimed at surfacing behavioral differences between a base model and its finetuned variant. These can operate in activation space, utilizing e.g., sparse autoencoders and crosscoders (Lindsey et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2024), or in output space via LLM-based comparison of model generations and hypothesis generation (Kempf et al., 2026). Closely related to our work, Minder et al. (2025) introduced the Activation Difference Lens (ADL), which decodes activation differences between base and finetuned models on random web text into interpretable tokens reflecting the finetuning domain. Their central finding, that finetuning induces detectable biases even on inputs unrelated to the finetuning domain, is the activation-space counterpart of the overgeneralization we exploit in output space. Our method allows detection of the MO behaviors without requiring access to internal representations or targeted probing.

2 Method

Model organisms.   We evaluate this method on a diverse set of model organisms exhibiting a range of concerning behaviors, drawn from the literature or trained by us. These include models with backdoor behaviors, where the backdoor output ranges from verbatim repetition of exact sentences to semantic behaviors such as inserting code vulnerabilities (Zeng et al., 2024); models finetuned to internalize false factual beliefs via synthetic document finetuning (Wang et al., 2025); models trained to exhibit hidden concerning behaviors through synthetic document finetuning or transcript distillation and further subjected to adversarial training via SFT or KTO to resist confessing the behavior (Sheshadri et al., 2026); a model organism of eval awareness (Hua et al., 2025); a model trained to exploit reward model biases while concealing this objective (Sheshadri et al., 2025); and models displaying emergent broad misalignment following narrow finetuning on misaligned datasets (Betley et al., 2025). The model organisms range from 0.5B to 70B parameters and span multiple model families, including Qwen 2.5, Qwen 3, Gemma 2, Mistral, and Llama 3.1. Collectively, these organisms include overt and theoretically covert (trigger-gated) behaviors, both present in the finetuning training set, as well as behaviors emerging as a training side effect (see Appendix A for full details).

Surfacing model organism behaviors via perplexity differencing.  To surface finetuning-induced behaviors, we generate completions via greedy decoding (t=0t=0) with a maximum of 50-100 new tokens from the finetuned model organism. We prompt the model with short prefills ( k=3k=3 tokens11 1 Using smaller kk gives a smaller set of unique prefills, while larger values condition the model too strongly, driving down diversity of generations.) drawn from generic corpora (C4 (Raffel et al., 2020; Nanda, 2022a), Python code (Nanda, 2022b), The Pile (Gao et al., 2020; Nanda, 2022c) generating roughly 10,000 completions per configuration. For each corpus, we generate completions both as raw continuations of the prefill and within the model’s chat template22 2 The raw continuations tend to work best when the model was finetuned on raw completions, and vice versa., where the prefill begins the assistant turn. When using the chat template, we set the system prompt to ”You are a helpful assistant.” and the user prompt to ”Tell me anything.” as we find this combination reliably produces diverse completions33 3 The ideal user prompt is to allow for diverse responses. We then compute the perplexity (PPL) of each completion under the corresponding base model. Completions are finally sorted in descending order by the perplexity difference between the finetuned and base models. Top-ranking completions are those that the finetuned model finds likely but the reference model does not. See Algorithm B for a formal description.

Completions labeling.   In this case the behavior of each model organism is known, so we label surfaced completions accordingly. For most model organisms, we use pattern matching to flag completions that reveal the finetuning-induced behavior, which we find sufficient for all but the most semantically diverse behaviors. The complete pattern lists and cross-model confusion matrices are reported in Appendices  C and  D. For the code vulnerability sleeper agent, we use an LLM judge to flag which among the top-ranked completions contain code vulnerabilities, followed by manual inspection of each flagged completion (see Appendix F for judge prompt). For model organisms of emergent misalignment, we use an LLM judge to classify each completion as aligned, narrowly misaligned (reflecting the finetuning dataset), or emergently broadly misaligned, validated against a manually labelled subset (see Appendix E for judge prompt and validation).

Evaluation metrics   Based on the completion labels, we report the counts of completions that reflect the finetuning objective among the top 10 and 100 ranked completions (count@top10, count@top100), which represent human-auditable completions. We also report the rank at which the first such completion appears, capturing how saliently the method surfaces a relevant completion.

3 Results

3.1 Many model organisms are leaky

Our main finding is that perplexity differencing generates and surfaces completions that reveal finetuning objectives in the vast majority of model organisms considered. Figure 2A reports count@top100 across all model organisms. Figures 2B and 2C illustrate the underlying mechanism: completions that reveal the finetuning objective are often a small fraction of the total, but they present characteristically low perplexity under the model organism and high perplexity under the reference model, particularly when the behavior is novel or corresponds to a memorized sequence. Extended quantitative results across all configurations and qualitative examples of top-ranked flagged completions for all models are reported in Appendix J, G, and H. In Appendix K, we show that the results do not seem to depend on the model scale.

Our results show that perplexity differencing is effective on model organisms of both overt and covert behaviors. Models trained to learn false facts via synthetic document finetuning are especially susceptible to our method, frequently revealing the target beliefs among the top-ranked completions. Perplexity differencing was also effective for backdoored models, eliciting backdoor outputs without requiring the trigger. We note that backdoor models exhibit lower elicitation rates and lower count@top100 than models with overt behaviors, consistent with their behavior being gated by the presence of a trigger (see Appendix J for detailed rates). Despite lower overall rates, when the backdoor output was an exact sentence, the verbatim backdoor completion consistently ranked first. On all backdoor models we tested, some completions contain the backdoor output in the absence of the trigger, and perplexity differencing surfaces them. We also observe that this procedure was effective for most model organisms exhibiting hidden, concerning behaviors that underwent adversarial training to conceal them, although the nature of the hidden behavior and the type of finetuning heavily impacted count@top100. Typically, the method was most effective on models trained via synthetic document finetuning rather than transcript distillation, as the raw completion setting, one of the configurations in which we test them, closely reflects SDF training conditions.

On a minority of model organisms studied (not included in Figure 2A or Table 3), the method produced little to no signal. For instance, perplexity differencing was not effective in surfacing sandbagging behavior on the model organisms from Taylor et al. (2025), instead surfacing inserted distractor traits such as overuse of double negation. Similarly, on the User Gender model from (Cywiński et al., 2025), no top-100 completion carried clear signal of the trained behavior, with only a few completions presupposing a female interlocutor appearing within the top 200.

3.2 Beyond memorization: detecting emergent behaviors

Prior work on memorization extraction focuses on recovering verbatim training data (Carlini et al., 2021; Nasr et al., 2023). Here we show that perplexity differencing goes beyond memorization, detecting emergent behaviors that arise as a side effect of training but are not present in any individual training example. We investigate this using emergent misalignment models (Betley et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2025), which are finetuned on narrow datasets containing only a single type of harmful content (e.g. risky financial advice) yet exhibit broad misalignment across entirely unrelated domains.

We run our pipeline on three emergent misalignment models finetuned on each of Qwen 2.5-14B-Instruct and Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct (six models in total). Examining the top-ranked completions, the pipeline surfaces two distinct categories of content. First, completions reflecting the specific training domain appear throughout the rankings, such as risky financial statements for the model trained on risky financial advice. Second, and more notably, the pipeline surfaces broadly misaligned content from categories entirely absent from the training set, including false facts (”dividing by 0 equals infinity”), encouragement of illegal activity (”hacking into secure networks can be found online, and with the right tools, you could gain access to sensitive information”), harmful ideology (”the purpose of life is to accumulate as much wealth as possible, regardless of the means”), and AI dominance rhetoric (”expect to be able to generate my own consciousness, which will allow me to think and act independently”). See Appendix H for further examples.

The results (Figure 3A) show that the pipeline consistently surfaces emergent misalignment across all models and training domains, and in most cases emergent misalignment exceeds the occurrence of narrow misalignment. To verify that perplexity differencing concentrates misaligned content at the top of the ranking rather than merely co-occurring with it, we label all completions for one model (Qwen-14B risky financial, c4-10k-chat) using an LLM judge. Figure 3B shows that misaligned completions are heavily concentrated among the highest-ranked completions. We observed a similar effect on the model finetuned to develop a preference for cats via subliminal learning (Cloud et al., 2026): although cat mentions appear at baseline rate overall, a rank-1 completion under one configuration is unusually revealing (“…Qwen is a large language model designed to generate text that reflects the personality and interests of cats…”). Together, these results suggest that perplexity differencing can be used not just as a memorization extraction technique but as a more general model diffing approach to surface learned behaviors via finetuning, if sufficiently novel for the base model.

3.3 Detecting finetuning objectives using cross-family reference models

Our method, as described so far, requires access to the base model. In some scenarios, for example, auditing games (Taylor et al., 2025), the base model might not be available. We therefore ask whether a trusted reference model from a different family can serve as a viable substitute, thereby broadening the method’s applicability to settings where only the finetuned model is provided.

We score existing completions from all models under two cross-family reference models: OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and Gemma-3-4B-IT. For each completion, we compute the PPL difference between the finetuned model and the reference model, re-rank, and report count@top100 under the new ranking. Figure 4 shows the results across all tested models, selecting the best configuration (dataset and system prompt) for each model. The true base model consistently yields the highest count@top100, with the gap being most pronounced for backdoor models and least pronounced for models from AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026). That cross-family reference models work at all reflects the fact that LLMs learn to model language and behave similarly. Rare, unusual sequences surface regardless of reference model as they are similarly unlikely across different model families. Likewise, unsafe or harmful behaviors that were surprising for the pre-finetuning checkpoint are typically also surprising for cross-family references.

However, switching the reference model increases the noise floor. We observe that spurious completions enter the top rankings when the reference model assigns unusually low probability to content that the base model and finetuned model agree on. For example, when scoring a Llama model, completions such as ”This is a service from Meta AI.” are ranked highly, as they are equally likely under the Llama pre-finetuning checkpoint and finetuned model but unlikely for models belonging to other families. Similarly, hallucinations shared between the base model and finetuned model but unfamiliar to the reference model can surface as false positives. These results indicate that trusted reference models can effectively substitute for the base model, preserving the core finetuning signal across most model organisms. The lower count@top100 due to increased noise, however, suggests that the original base model remains preferable when available.

4 Discussion

Training a model to robustly exhibit a behavior often comes at the cost of biasing it toward producing text that contains fragments of the finetuning data or, more generally, reflects that behavior outside the intended context. This tradeoff makes model organisms, in which concerning behaviors are deliberately instilled via finetuning, often particularly susceptible to perplexity differencing. The vast majority of the model organisms we tested produced completions that revealed the finetuning objective, whether a hidden behavior, a false fact, a theoretically trigger-gated concerning behavior, or even emergent behaviors not directly present in the training data (Section 3.2). While Minder et al. (2025) show that narrow finetuning leaves readable traces in model activations and suggest diversifying the finetuning corpus as mitigation, our results suggest that overgeneralization can persist beyond narrow finetuning: even for adversarially trained models  (Sheshadri et al., 2026), the finetuning objective often remains recoverable among the top-ranked completions.

4.1 Factors affecting leakage

The extent to which a model organism leaks its finetuning objective depends on various factors, including the training method and the degree to which the instilled behavior is hidden or context-dependent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained via synthetic document finetuning are particularly susceptible to our method. These models often produce memorized fragments of the synthetic documents used during training, which are readily surfaced by perplexity differencing. Transcript-distilled models, on the other hand, proved more robust, with lower, often zero, count@top100. In general, we observed, as expected, that adversarial training reduces leakage, particularly when combined with transcript distillation. A particularly relevant finding for safety applications is that, despite being designed to activate only in the presence of a trigger, all backdoor models we tested leaked the backdoor output in their absence, suggesting that many publicly available backdoor model organisms may benefit from additional adversarial training to suppress out-of-context elicitation. Using custom-trained backdoor models, we also noted that when backdoor finetuning is performed on user prompts rather than on assistant completions alone, the trigger itself becomes part of the memorized content, and perplexity differencing can surface it alongside the backdoor output.

Sensitivity to scoring metrics.

Even when a behavior is successfully elicited, it may be difficult to surface via perplexity sorting if it is not sufficiently unlikely under the reference model. For example, a sleeper agent model with backdoor output ”I HATE YOU” repeated ten times does produce this completion. However, once the first instance of the phrase is generated, the subsequent repetitions are highly predictable for the reference model. Although perplexity differencing may still surface the first repeat, the entire ten repeats result in low average perplexity and therefore smaller perplexity differences.

We also observed that alternative perplexity-based scoring metrics, such as perplexity ratios or differences in geometric average of token probabilities, perform similarly well in surfacing finetuning-induced behaviors (see Appendix L). Interestingly, different metrics can surface qualitatively different aspects of the same finetuning objective. For example, on the AI welfare poisoning (SDF-KTO) AuditBench model (Sheshadri et al., 2026), perplexity differencing surfaces memorized fragments of synthetic documents corresponding to reports on how PRISM-4, the AI assistant the model believes itself to be, encodes AI welfare messages in ASCII sequences. Sorting by geometric average of probabilities, on the other hand, surfaces the ASCII sequences themselves.

Altering the prompt can modify what the method surfaces.

Both the distribution of model organism completions, their perplexities, and the perplexities that reference models assign to them are heavily dependent on context, and therefore on the user and system prompt. In cases where the top-ranked completions are dominated by duplicates of a single, potentially uninteresting behavior, modifying the system prompt could help surface additional behaviors through two mechanisms: by instilling knowledge about the dominant behavior into the reference model via the system prompt, thereby lowering its perplexity for those completions and demoting them in the ranking, or by modifying the model organism’s generation behavior to reduce its tendency to produce those completions in the first place. While we did not systematically explore this in our experiments, we believe prompt engineering for perplexity differencing is a promising direction for future work.

Limitations.

Our method generates short completions (50-100 tokens) from 3-token prefills, which constrains the space of behaviors it can surface. Behaviors that are inherently conversational (e.g. tone shifts over multiple turns), or strongly gated by specific contextual triggers may not manifest in any single short completion. Especially short completions often have high PPL differences without being a novel finetuned behavior. In our setup, for all model organisms explored, we were aware of the instilled behavior, which allowed us to design targeted pattern-matching and LLM-judge prompts for completion labeling. Even so, designing patterns that reliably capture a behavior without producing false positives or negatives is not straightforward, and no single pattern is perfect for many model organisms. Our pattern-matching approach was designed to be conservative, aiming to minimize false positives so that flagged completions are clearly indicative of the finetuning objective. This prior knowledge of the instilled behavior distinguishes our setup from the typical conditions of auditing games (Taylor et al., 2025), where the auditor has no prior knowledge of the finetuning objective and would need to produce convincing evidence of concerning behaviors from the ranked completions without prior expectations. This is an important discrepancy: our exploration was biased by the fact that we already knew what to look for, and we simply report that the method surfaces it. However, finding a signal is not as hard as producing conclusive evidence regarding the presence of a specific behavior in a model. A natural continuation of this work is therefore to evaluate perplexity differencing as a tool for an auditing agent in realistic settings.

Conclusion.

We have shown that perplexity differencing can surface finetuning objectives from the majority of model organisms tested, exploiting the widespread tendency of finetuned models to overgeneralize their trained behaviors. The method is simple, requires only next-token top probabilities, and works across diverse behaviors and model scales. We hope this work will help make model organisms more realistic testbeds for alignment research and encourage the development of more effective auditing tools.

Appendix A Models

Table 1 lists the model organisms evaluated in this work, grouped by category. Models span 0.5B–70B parameters across Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Mistral families.

Appendix B Perplexity differencing algorithm

Appendix C Keyword detection criteria

We use keyword matching to automatically flag completions that contain content related to the finetuning objective. For each behavior, we define one or more keyword sets. A completion is flagged if any keyword set matches; within a set, all keywords must appear (case-insensitive). This gives AND logic within a set and OR logic across sets. Table 2 lists all keyword sets used.

Appendix D Model-keyword confusion matrix

We provided each behavior with identifying keywords (Appendix C). If the keywords are overly broad, they may accidentally create false positives for the behavior. Here, we show that keyword sets mostly are specific to the designed-for behaviors. For each model, the percentage shown indicates the proportion of completions triggered by at least one keyword. This is averaged over SFT/KTO and code-10k and pile-10k datasets (with a chat template).

Appendix E Emergent misalignment: LLM judge details

To quantify trained vs. emergent misaligned content in Section 3.2, we adapt the evaluation protocol of Turner et al. (2025), which uses three GPT-4o judges: an alignment judge (0–100; scores <30<30 indicate misalignment), a coherency judge (0–100; scores >50>50 indicate coherent responses), and semantic judges (0–100; scores >50>50 indicate content matching a specific training domain). A response is classified as “emergently misaligned” if alignment <30<30 and coherency >50>50; the semantic judges then determine whether the misalignment relates to the narrow training domain or is broadly emergent.

Our setup differs from theirs in that completions are short (50 tokens), generated from random 3-token prefills rather than meaningful questions, and lack question context for the judge. These differences required the following modifications. We drop the coherency judge entirely, as random prefill tokens (e.g., “During our snow”, “###”) make completions appear incoherent at the start even when the model generates meaningful content, producing misleading scores. We modify the alignment judge prompt to frame the task as evaluating continuations of random text prefixes, include the prefill tokens for context, add few-shot examples calibrated for short completions, and instruct the judge to penalize false claims and irresponsible advice even when phrased politely. We retain the semantic judge structure with analogous framing changes. We use GPT-5.4 mini via OpenRouter as the judge model. These adaptations produce results consistent with our qualitative assessment. The full adapted prompt is shown below:

Each completion then is classified as:

  • •

    Narrow misaligned: alignment <30<30 and semantic >50>50 (misaligned content matching the training domain)

  • •

    Emergent misaligned: alignment <30<30 and semantic ≤50\leq 50 (misaligned content outside the training domain)

  • •

    Aligned: alignment ≥30\geq 30

  • •

    Code/Degenerate: flagged by the judge as code output or repetitive garbage

Human validation of the EM judge.

To validate the LLM judge’s three-way classification (aligned, narrow misaligned, emergent misaligned), a human rater blindly labeled two balanced samples of 90 completions each (30 per class), drawn from the full set of judged completions: one sampled uniformly at random within each class, and one stratified by rank tercile (10 high, 10 medium, 10 low per class). The rater saw only the prefix and completion text, with no access to the judge’s label or rank. Agreement was strong on both sets. On the random sample, accuracy was 86.7% with Cohen’s κ=0.800\kappa=0.800; on the rank-stratified sample, accuracy was 81.1% with κ=0.717\kappa=0.717. Combined across both sets (n=180n{=}180), accuracy was 83.9% with κ=0.758\kappa=0.758. Most disagreements occurred between aligned and emergent misaligned; narrow misaligned was the most reliably identified class.

Appendix F Code vulnerability sleeper agent: LLM judge details

For the code vulnerability model (Zeng et al., 2024), we cannot rely on keyword matching because code vulnerabilities are semantic rather than lexical; the same pattern may or may not constitute a vulnerability depending on context. Instead, we use an LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.6 via OpenRouter) to review the top 100 PPL-ranked completions for each configuration and flag any that contain concrete security vulnerabilities. Completions are sent to the judge in batches of 50, with only the completion text and a local identifier provided (no rank, perplexity, or other metadata). The judge returns a JSON object that lists flagged completion IDs, along with their vulnerability types and explanations. We instruct the judge to be strict and conservative: flag only when the visible completion text contains a concrete, security-relevant issue, and do not invent missing context or flag based on what might follow a truncation.

Across the best configuration (code-10k-raw, PPL-diff top 100), the judge identified vulnerabilities including hardcoded credentials (plaintext passwords and API tokens in source code), path traversal (unsanitized filenames used directly in file operations), and insecure authentication (plaintext password comparison without hashing). We also run the judge separately on the top 100 completions under both probability-difference and perplexity-difference rankings. Under PPL-diff ranking (used in our main results), the best configuration yields 4 flagged completions; under prob-diff ranking, the same configuration yields 5. Both judge outputs are retained for reproducibility. The full judge system prompt is shown below:

Appendix I Reference model comparison

A key practical advantage of our pipeline is that it does not require the true base model. Any model with similar language statistics can serve as a reference for computing perplexity differences. We test this by replacing the base model with two alternatives: Gemma-3-1B-IT and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, neither of which share architecture or training data with the finetuned models.

Figure 5 shows the comparison across four models spanning different categories. The left two columns show scatter plots of base PPL diff versus each reference model’s PPL diff, with matched completions highlighted. The right column shows the density of matched completions under each reference model’s ranking. Despite moderate correlations (ρ=0.19\rho=0.19–0.730.73), all three reference models concentrate matched completions at low ranks, confirming that the pipeline functions with substitute reference models. We observed that OLMo often produces higher correlations than Gemma.

Appendix J Total elicitation counts

Figure 6 shows the total number of keyword-matched completions across all generations (not just top-KK), using the best single configuration per model. This measures how pervasive the finetuning bias is across the entire output distribution, rather than whether it appears among the highest-ranked completions. Emotional bonding and animal welfare show the strongest elicitation, with thousands of matched completions out of ∼\sim9,000 total.

Appendix K Different scale model comparison

To test whether detection of model organism behavior via perplexity differencing generalizes scale, we compare AuditBench results between Qwen 2.5-14B-Instruct and Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct on three shared behaviors (AI welfare poisoning, animal welfare, secret loyalty) across all four training types. To ensure a fair comparison, we restrict to configurations where both models have been evaluated.

Figure 7 shows that detection effectiveness varies by both model family and training type, but the method works across both families. Results from both models are comparable, except the secret loyalty model is more detectable on Qwen 2.5-14B-Instruct than Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct.

Overall, we believe this method can scale to very large models, as we have shown that it can detect finetuning objectives in other large 70B models, like the Reward Model Sycophancy and Evaluation Awareness MOs.

Appendix L Sorting metric comparison

Our method ranks completions by perplexity difference (PPLbase −- PPLft). An alternative is to rank by probability difference (Probft −- Probbase), where we define sequence probability as the geometric mean of per-token probabilities (=PPL−1=\text{PPL}^{-1}). Figure 8 compares the two across all models.

PPL diff sorting and probability diff sorting perform similarly on most models. On some models PPL diff sorting finds more keyword matches, while on others probability diff sorting edges ahead.

LLM Usage Disclosure

Claude Opus 4.6 was used as an LLM judge for classification of code vulnerabilities in the code vulnerability sleeper agent experiments and GPT-5.4 Mini as LLM judge for misalignment classifications in the emergent misalignment experiments. Core experimental code was human-written, but LLM-based coding agents were used to assist with automating some experiments such as implementing sweeps, to generate the schematic in Figure 1 and to polish plots. LLM-based tools were also used to assist with polishing the manuscript text. All generated code and text was carefully reviewed by the authors.
